407.title: Bold outside, careful inside
407.hook: be confident about outside things and cautious about your own judgments (Discourses 2.1)
407.howItsDone: Stoic readers often use this chapter to sort their fears, acting boldly on outside things they've been avoiding while slowing down their own quick judgments.

segments.voice: Yesterday: stand firm, roots holding while the branches move. Where did you stay steady under pressure? Day four hundred seven.

Hunters in the ancient world had a clever trick for catching deer. They'd string a line of feathers across the woods. The feathers fluttered, the deer panicked and ran the other way, straight into the nets the hunters had set. The deer weren't cowards. They were afraid of the wrong thing, and fearless about the wrong thing. Epictetus thought most of us live exactly like those deer. Today: bold outside, careful inside.
screen: `A LINE OF FEATHERS.` → `THE DEER RUN INTO THE NETS.` → `AFRAID OF THE WRONG THING.`

segments.voice: This opens book two of the Discourses, chapter one: that confidence isn't at odds with caution. The Stoics claimed you should be both, completely bold and completely careful, and people thought that sounded like nonsense. Epictetus explains. Be careful, he says, where the real danger is: in your own will. That's where you can actually go wrong, by agreeing too fast, wanting the wrong thing, acting on a bad impression. And be bold about everything outside the will, because nothing out there can make you bad. Then he shows how we flip it. We're terrified of things outside us: death, exile, pain, losing face. And we're reckless inside: careless with our judgments, quick to agree with any thought that comes along. Like the deer, fleeing the feathers and running into the nets. Epictetus has another image for the outside fears. Death and pain, he says, are like the masks that scare little children. Turn the mask around and look at the back. It doesn't bite. What frightens us is mostly our opinion about death and pain, not the things themselves. This doesn't mean being careless with your health or your safety; Epictetus would still have you look both ways crossing the street. It means putting your carefulness where it does the most good, on your own judgments, and letting your courage go out into the world.
screen: `BOTH BOLD AND CAREFUL.` · `CAREFUL WHERE THE REAL DANGER IS.` · `WE FLIP IT, LIKE THE DEER.` · `TURN THE MASK AROUND.` · then, large: `BOLD OUTSIDE, CAREFUL INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of one outside thing you've been avoiding out of fear: a phone call, a conversation, applying for something, speaking up. Look at it like a mask, and turn it around. What's actually on the back? Usually it's discomfort, not disaster. Then turn inward and notice one place you've been careless: a judgment you made too fast, an assumption you never checked. Hold both. Bold out there, careful in here. The bell holds the time.
Bold outside. Epictetus' answer to the Stoic paradox: be confident about what's outside your will, and save your caution for your own judgments.
Your line: bold outside, careful inside. Today, be bold about one outside thing you've been dodging, and careful with one judgment before you act on it. Day four hundred seven.

408.title: Play the ball well
408.hook: players care about handling the ball well, not about the ball (Discourses 2.5)
408.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners often separate the outcome of a task from the way they do it, and judge their day by the quality of their effort, an idea many trace to the ball players of this chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bold outside, the deer and the feathers. Which outside thing were you bold about? Day four hundred eight.

Watch a pickup basketball game in a park. Nobody stops to argue about whether the ball is a good ball or a bad ball. It's just the ball. Everything they care about is what they do with it: the pass, the catch, the footwork, the shot. A great player with a scuffed, half-flat ball is still a joy to watch. Epictetus watched ball games too, and he saw in them the answer to one of the hardest puzzles in Stoic thought. Today: play the ball well.
screen: `NOBODY ARGUES ABOUT THE BALL.` → `THE PASS, THE CATCH, THE SHOT.` → `A HARD STOIC PUZZLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle. The Stoics said outside things, money, health, even life itself, are neither good nor bad. Only how we use them is. So why care about anything? Why not shrug at everything? That's Discourses book two, chapter five: how greatness of mind fits with carefulness. And Epictetus answers with games. Look at people playing dice, he says. The dice don't matter, the counters don't matter, and you can't control what falls. But using well what falls: that's your job, and you can do it with real care. Then the ball players. None of them argues about whether the ball is good or bad. They argue about throwing and catching, and there they're all skill, speed and attention. Then he goes to the most serious ball game he knows. Socrates, at his trial, knew how to play ball. And what was the ball? Life. Prison. Exile. Drinking poison. Being taken from his wife, and leaving his children without a father. Those were the things he was handed, and he played with them, Epictetus says, and handled them with good form. So the answer to the puzzle is this: don't treat the ball as everything, and don't treat the game as nothing. Pour all your care into the playing. Let the ball be the ball. A job, a diagnosis, a family situation: those are what's been tossed to you. How you catch them and pass them on is where the skill lives.
screen: `THE PUZZLE: WHY CARE?` · `THE DICE DON'T MATTER, THE PLAY DOES.` · `SOCRATES KNEW HOW TO PLAY BALL.` · `ALL YOUR CARE GOES INTO THE PLAYING.` · then, large: `PLAY THE BALL WELL.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of one task waiting for you today, ordinary or hard. Notice what you're hoping it gets you: praise, a result, a relief. That's the ball. Set it down, just for now. Then picture yourself doing the task itself with full care: the first step, the attention, the craft of it. Feel the difference between playing for the prize and playing well. Rest in that. The bell holds the time.
Play the ball well. Epictetus' answer to why we should care about things that aren't the good: the ball doesn't matter, but how you play it does.
Your line: play the ball well. Pick one task today and play it with full care, for the skill of it, not for the prize. Day four hundred eight.

409.title: Who am I here?
409.hook: remember who you are, a human, a citizen, a son, a brother, and act from each (Discourses 2.10)
409.howItsDone: Many Stoic readers pause before entering a room or conversation to name the role they're stepping into, and ask what it asks of them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: play the ball well, Socrates handling what he was tossed. Which task did you play for the skill, not the prize? Day four hundred nine.

In a single afternoon you might be a manager in a meeting, a customer on hold, a daughter on the phone with her mother, a neighbor waving across the fence, and a stranger letting someone merge in traffic. Each one asks something slightly different of you. Most of us switch between them without noticing, and sometimes we bring the wrong one into the room: the boss into the family dinner, the tired customer into the conversation with a friend. Epictetus had a method for this. Today: who am I here?
screen: `MANAGER, CUSTOMER, DAUGHTER, NEIGHBOR.` → `EACH ASKS SOMETHING DIFFERENT.` → `THE WRONG ONE IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter ten: how to find what you owe from the names you carry. Consider who you are, Epictetus says. First, a human being, which means someone with a will, and nothing in you ranks higher than that. Second, a citizen of the world, a part of it, and not a minor part. So act the way a hand or a foot would act if it could think: never just for itself, always as part of the whole body. Then the names get closer to home. Remember you're a son, he tells his students, who were young men. What does that name ask? To treat what's yours as belonging to the family, to give way to your father, never to speak badly of him to others. Remember you're a brother. That name asks you to yield, to be courteous, and never to fight your brother over things that don't really matter. Then, he says, if you sit on a city council, remember you're a councilor. If you're young, remember you're young. If old, old. If a father, a father. Each name, if you stop and think about it, tells you what to do. He spoke to sons and brothers because that's who was in the room. The method fits daughters, sisters, parents, partners, coworkers, anyone. And it's simple enough to use at a doorway: before you walk in, ask which name you're carrying into this room, and what that name asks of you.
screen: `FIRST, A HUMAN BEING.` · `A CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.` · `SON, BROTHER, COUNCILOR, FATHER.` · `EACH NAME TELLS YOU WHAT TO DO.` · then, large: `WHO AM I HERE?`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of the next place you'll walk into today: an office, a kitchen, a classroom, a call. Name who you'll be there: parent, colleague, friend, customer, neighbor. Now ask what that name asks of you. Patience? Honesty? Generosity? Leadership? Let one quality come forward. Picture yourself crossing the doorway carrying that name, and acting from it. The bell holds the time.
Who am I here? Epictetus' method of names: human, citizen of the world, child, sibling, parent. Each name tells you what you owe.
Your line: who am I here. At one doorway today, pause and ask it, then act well from that one role. Day four hundred nine.

410.title: Start with weakness
410.hook: philosophy begins with noticing your own weakness (Discourses 2.11)
410.howItsDone: Many people who practice Stoicism begin by naming an area where they feel certain but may be wrong, and treat that honest admission as the start of their training.

segments.voice: Yesterday: who am I here, the names you carry through the day. Which role did you step into on purpose? Day four hundred ten.

Nobody walks into a calculus class insisting they already know calculus. Nobody sits down at a piano for the first time convinced they can play Chopin. With those things, we know what we don't know. But ask a room full of people what's fair, what a good life is, or how to treat a difficult relative, and almost everyone is sure they already know. Epictetus found that strange, and he said it's exactly where philosophy has to begin. Today: start with weakness.
screen: `NOBODY THINKS THEY KNOW CALCULUS.` → `EVERYONE KNOWS WHAT'S FAIR.` → `WHERE PHILOSOPHY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter eleven: what the beginning of philosophy is. For anyone who comes in by the right door, Epictetus says, it begins with noticing your own weakness and inability in the things that matter most. Why there? He explains with geometry and music. Nobody is born with an idea of a right triangle, or of a musical interval. We learn those from teachers, so nobody who hasn't learned them thinks they know them. But good and bad, fair and unfair, noble and shameful: everyone arrives with some sense of those. We're born with the outline. And because we have the outline, we assume we know how to fill it in. That's the trap. Two people can both love justice and still disagree completely about what's just in a given case. So who's right? You can't both be. Seeming right to yourself isn't enough; people who are wrong feel just as certain. So philosophy, he says, starts by admitting that, and then looking for a standard, the way people invented scales for weight and rulers for length, so that arguments could be settled by something outside our feelings. It's an oddly hopeful beginning. Weakness here doesn't mean you're bad. It means you're honest about being unfinished. The person who says, I don't actually know how to handle my anger, is further along than the person who's sure they've got it figured out.
screen: `THE RIGHT DOOR IN.` · `NO ONE IS BORN KNOWING GEOMETRY.` · `WE ALL THINK WE KNOW WHAT'S GOOD.` · `LOOK FOR A STANDARD.` · then, large: `START WITH WEAKNESS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe. Ask yourself, gently: where am I sure I'm right, and might not be? Maybe about a person, a decision, a way of doing things. Let one come up. Don't argue with it yet. Just say to yourself, plainly: here, I'm not as strong as I think. Notice how that feels: maybe uncomfortable, maybe a strange relief. Then breathe, and let the admission be a beginning. The bell holds the time.
Start with weakness. Epictetus' door into philosophy: noticing that in the things that matter most, we're less sure and less able than we think.
Your line: start with weakness. Today, admit one weakness, to yourself or to someone you trust, and treat it as a starting line. Day four hundred ten.

411.title: Without the crowd
411.hook: the singer is only anxious when he wants the crowd's applause (Discourses 2.13)
411.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners often meet nerves by asking what they want that isn't in their control, usually approval, and turning their attention back to doing the task well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: start with weakness, the door into philosophy. Was there a weakness you admitted, even quietly? Day four hundred eleven.

In the shower, you can sing. Really sing. Full voice, the high note, the whole song. Then someone hands you a microphone at a wedding and your throat closes up. Your voice didn't change between the bathroom and the reception hall. Your skill didn't change. Something else walked into the room with you. Epictetus noticed this two thousand years ago, watching musicians in the theater, and he named exactly what it was. Today: without the crowd.
screen: `IN THE SHOWER, YOU CAN SING.` → `A MICROPHONE AT A WEDDING.` → `SOMETHING ELSE WALKED IN.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter thirteen, on anxiety. Epictetus starts like a doctor making a diagnosis. When I see someone anxious, he says, I ask: what does this person want? Because if they didn't want something outside their control, why would they be anxious? Then the musician. A lyre player singing by himself isn't anxious at all. But when he walks into the theater, even if he has a fine voice and plays beautifully, he's anxious. Why? Because he doesn't only want to sing well. He wants to be applauded, and that isn't up to him. Where his skill is, there's confidence. Bring in a crowd he wants something from, and the anxiety arrives. Epictetus then gives a pair of real people. When Zeno, the founder of the Stoic school, went to see King Antigonus, Zeno wasn't anxious. Antigonus was. The king wanted to impress the philosopher; the philosopher wanted nothing from the king. The one with the power was the one sweating. The fix isn't to stop caring about doing well. Practice your craft, Epictetus says; get good. The fix is to notice when part of you is singing for the applause, and to bring the attention back to the singing. You can stand in a full room and still, inside, be singing without the crowd.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE ANXIOUS ONE WANT?` · `ALONE: NO ANXIETY. THE THEATER: ANXIETY.` · `ZENO CALM, THE KING ANXIOUS.` · `BACK TO THE SINGING.` · then, large: `WITHOUT THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of something coming up that makes you nervous: a presentation, a date, a meeting, a post. Ask Epictetus' question: what do I want here that isn't up to me? Their approval? Their applause? Name it. Then picture doing the thing as if no one were watching, the way you sing in the shower. Feel the difference in your chest. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Without the crowd. Epictetus' diagnosis of nerves: the singer alone is calm; the anxiety comes with wanting applause, which was never up to him.
Your line: without the crowd. Do one thing today with no audience at all, and notice how it feels to do it just to do it well. Day four hundred eleven.

412.title: Habits grow by use
412.hook: walk to become a walker, read to become a reader (Discourses 2.18)
412.howItsDone: Stoic practitioners often pick one small virtue to practice repeatedly, on the principle that each act strengthens the habit, and replace an unwanted habit with a chosen one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: without the crowd, the singer alone and the singer in the theater. What did you do with no audience at all? Day four hundred twelve.

After a week in bed with the flu, you get up and try to walk to the mailbox. Your legs feel like someone else's. A week ago you didn't think about walking at all. Now it takes effort. Nothing was injured. You just didn't use them, and they quietly got weaker. Epictetus used almost exactly that example, a person getting out of bed after ten days, to explain how everything in us grows or shrinks. Today: habits grow by use.
screen: `A WEEK IN BED WITH THE FLU.` → `LEGS LIKE SOMEONE ELSE'S.` → `NOTHING INJURED, JUST UNUSED.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter eighteen. Every habit and every ability, Epictetus says, is kept up and made stronger by the actions that match it. Walking by walking. Running by running. If you want to be a good reader, read. If you want to be a writer, write. Stop reading for thirty days, he says, and do something else instead, and you'll see what happens. Lie in bed for ten days, then get up and try a long walk, and you'll see how weak your legs have become. So here's his rule, as plain as anything in the Discourses. If you want to be able to do something, make a habit of doing it. If you don't want to do something, don't do it, and get used to doing something else in its place. Notice that second half. He doesn't just say stop. He says replace. A habit leaves a space, and something will fill it. Then he turns from the body to the mind, which for him is the whole point. Patience, honesty, gentleness, courage: these work the same way. Each kind act makes the next one easier. Each honest answer makes honesty more natural. And the other direction too: every time you give in to a bad reaction, you haven't just had one bad moment; you've strengthened the habit. Nobody becomes patient by reading about patience. You become patient the way you become a walker: one ordinary step at a time.
screen: `WALKING BY WALKING.` · `TEN DAYS IN BED, WEAK LEGS.` · `DON'T JUST STOP: REPLACE.` · `PATIENCE GROWS THE SAME WAY.` · then, large: `HABITS GROW BY USE.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Choose one good act you'd like to grow: listening without interrupting, a kind word at the door, putting the phone away at dinner, pausing before you answer. Something small. Picture yourself doing it once today. Then picture doing it again tomorrow, and the day after. Feel how the second time is a little easier than the first. That's the muscle. Rest with it. The bell holds the time.
Habits grow by use. Epictetus' rule: walk to become a walker, read to become a reader, and act patiently to become patient.
Your line: habits grow by use. Repeat one good act today, on purpose, and let the repetition do the work. Day four hundred twelve.

413.title: Count the calm days
413.hook: count the days you weren't angry: every day, then every other, then every third (Discourses 2.18)
413.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a private tally of days without anger, expecting setbacks and watching the gaps between angry days grow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: habits grow by use, walk to become a walker. Which good act did you repeat on purpose? Day four hundred thirteen, the end of the week.

You've probably got a streak going somewhere. Days on a language app. Days on this path. Steps on a watch. There's something about a number going up that keeps people showing up. It turns out the idea is old. Nearly two thousand years ago, Epictetus gave his students a streak to keep, not for steps or lessons, but for something much harder: the days they got through without losing their temper. Today: count the calm days.
screen: `A STREAK GOING SOMEWHERE.` → `A NUMBER GOING UP.` → `DAYS WITHOUT LOSING YOUR TEMPER.`

segments.voice: This is the same chapter as yesterday, Discourses book two, chapter eighteen, where habits grow by use. If you don't want to be quick-tempered, Epictetus says, then don't feed the habit. Don't give it anything that makes it grow. And at first, keep quiet and count the days you weren't angry. I used to be angry every day. Now every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth. And if you make it to thirty days, he says, offer thanks to God, because the habit is first weakened, and then it's wiped out. Notice how kind this is. He doesn't say, never get angry again starting today. He expects relapses. Every other day is progress. Every third day is more. He's measuring the gaps between angry days getting longer. In the same chapter he gives a tool for the moment the anger rises. When an impression hits you hard, he says, don't let it carry you off. Say to it: wait for me a little, impression. Let me see what you are, and what you're about. Let me test you. That little pause is how the count goes up. And there's a detail that's easy to miss. He tells them to keep quiet about it. Count privately. This isn't a streak to post. Look back at the week: bold outside, play the ball well, who am I here, start with weakness, without the crowd, habits grow by use. And today, count the calm days.
screen: `DON'T FEED THE HABIT.` · `EVERY DAY, EVERY OTHER, EVERY THIRD.` · `WAIT FOR ME A LITTLE, IMPRESSION.` · `COUNT QUIETLY.` · then, large: `COUNT THE CALM DAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think back over today, or yesterday if today has barely started. Was there anger in it? A flash, a slow burn, a sharp word? Notice without judging. If the day was calm, let yourself feel that, quietly: one mark on the count. If it wasn't, no scolding; the count simply starts again. Then rehearse the pause: imagine a hot moment, and hear yourself say, wait a little. Let me see what you are. The bell holds the time.
Count the calm days. Epictetus' plan for a quick temper: angry every day, then every other, then every third, until thirty calm days in a row.
Your line: count the calm days. Tonight, if today was calm, mark it privately and start the count. Day four hundred thirteen, and a week done.
